name: Fingerprint linkability research — the cluster comprising FP-STALKER (Vastel, Laperdrix, Rudametkin, Rouvoy; IEEE S&P 2018), FP-Radar (Nikkhah Bahrami, Iqbal, Shafiq; PoPETs 2022(2)), and EFF's Cover Your Tracks (formerly Panopticlick, 2010; renamed 2020). Read alongside its necessary corrective, Gomez-Boix et al., 'Hiding in the Crowd' (WWW 2018). Sometimes referenced collectively as 'fingerprint evolution / linkability' literature.
kind: Research results plus one public measurement service. FP-STALKER is a linking algorithm (rule-based and hybrid random-forest variants) with released code; FP-Radar is a longitudinal measurement-and-detection pipeline; Cover Your Tracks is a live, EFF-operated self-test service that doubles as a data-collection instrument. None is a library this project would import; all three are oracles for reasoning about what a long-lived sensor discloses across sessions.
maturity: FP-STALKER: research prototype, 2018, code archived on GitHub, not maintained as a product — but the technique is unquestionably in production at commercial fingerprinting vendors (FingerprintJS Pro, DataDome, Castle) who sell exactly 'stable visitor ID across fingerprint drift' as the product. FP-Radar: research prototype, 2022, code public (pooneh-nb/fp-radar-public), no production deployment known. Cover Your Tracks: production service, continuously operated by EFF since 2010, though its underlying uniqueness corpus and test battery lag the current fingerprinting surface.
license: FP-STALKER code is released for research use (MIT-family) [uncertain — exact SPDX identifier not verified]. FP-Radar code is public on GitHub under a permissive license [uncertain]. Cover Your Tracks is GPL-family, EFF-authored, and in any case is used as a service rather than vendored. Nothing here is a licensing obstacle for this project because nothing here would be linked into the fold; the artifacts of interest are the numbers and the threat model, which carry no license.
keeps_and_discards: This item does not extract page content at all — it is the adversary's side of the ledger, and its relevance is that it tells you what a browser-resident sensor emits whether or not it intends to. FP-STALKER consumes a fixed attribute vector (user agent, accept headers, timezone, screen resolution, plugin and font lists, canvas hash, WebGL vendor/renderer, local storage and DNT flags, platform, cookie support) and discards page content entirely. FP-Radar consumes JavaScript source recovered from the Wayback Machine, reduces each script to an AST, and keeps only the set of web-API keywords touched, discarding all data flow, all values, and all DOM interaction — a keyword bag over time. Cover Your Tracks keeps a ~20-signal vector plus the tracker-blocking behaviour observed on its own probe requests. In every case, what survives is a low-dimensional identity vector, and what is discarded is everything this project actually cares about: content, structure, ordering, text.
structure_preserved: None, and the absence is the point. No nesting, no ordering, no tabular relations, no shadow boundaries survive any of these pipelines — they are collapse-to-a-vector by design. FP-Radar's temporal co-occurrence graph is the only structure any of them builds, and it is structure over APIs-across-time, not over documents: nodes are API keywords, edges are co-occurrence within a script, and clusters are read as fingerprinting 'techniques'. That graph is genuinely interesting to this project as a shape — an incrementally-updatable co-occurrence structure over a symbol alphabet — but it carries no document structure whatsoever, and it is built offline over a decade of crawls rather than online over one page.
interactive_elements: Not handled as content. Controls matter to this literature only as fingerprint surfaces: FP-STALKER treats no control state as a feature. The adjacent behavioural-biometrics line (mouse dynamics, keystroke timing, scroll cadence) does read interaction, and it is precisely what a Marionette-driven sensor fails, but that is a different technique family and is not part of FP-STALKER/FP-Radar/Cover Your Tracks. The relevant transfer to this project is negative: an actuator that clicks controls at machine-uniform cadence is more linkable across sessions than the static fingerprint is, and no amount of static hardening touches that.
interactive_state_fidelity: Not applicable in the extraction sense — none of these preserves disabled / checked / selected / expanded / aria state, because none reads the DOM as a document. The one indirect bearing on this project's 'tag plus interactivity' bet is that interactivity affordances themselves (which elements are focusable, which respond to pointer events) are not part of any published fingerprint vector, so recording interactivity in the fold adds no measurable linkability. The token cost is zero here because the token budget question does not arise.
layout_awareness: FP-STALKER reads screen resolution and available screen dimensions as attributes, and Cover Your Tracks reads screen size, colour depth and (via CSS media queries) viewport characteristics. This is geometry as an identity attribute, not geometry as document structure — it is read once, coarsely, at the window level, and never per-node. That distinction matters for this project: the fold's refusal to read layout is unaffected by any of this work, but the actuator's window and viewport dimensions ARE a first-class fingerprint attribute, and a non-default or unusual window size (a headless default of 800x600, a maximised 4K viewport, a viewport with no scrollbar allowance) is one of the higher-entropy attributes in every study that measures it.
javascript_required: FP-STALKER's attribute vector is roughly half HTTP-header-derived and half JavaScript-derived; the canvas, WebGL, font-enumeration and audio attributes all require script execution, and they are the high-entropy half. FP-Radar requires no script execution at analysis time — it parses recovered script source statically — but its entire subject matter is scripts that run. Cover Your Tracks degrades gracefully with JS disabled and reports a correspondingly lower (and, ironically, sometimes more distinctive) fingerprint. For this project the consequence is direct and uncomfortable: a real browser reading a real page runs the page's scripts, so every fingerprinting script on the page fires, and the fold's no-mocks constraint therefore guarantees maximal fingerprint disclosure. There is no configuration in which the sensor reads a live page and does not emit a fingerprint.
evaluation_method: FP-STALKER: a longitudinal re-identification task. Fingerprints are collected repeatedly from consented browser instances via an extension; the algorithm is then asked, for each new fingerprint, whether it belongs to a known browser instance or is new. The headline metric is 'average maximum tracking duration' — how many days a browser instance can be followed before the linking chain breaks — evaluated by replaying the collection timeline, with a rule-based variant and a hybrid random-forest variant compared against Eckersley's earlier heuristic. FP-Radar: unsupervised. It crawls historical script snapshots from the Wayback Machine for top-100K sites over roughly a decade, builds an AST-derived API-keyword co-occurrence graph per time slice, embeds and clusters it, and treats cluster membership plus temporal trajectory as the fingerprinting signal; validation is by comparison against existing fingerprinting detectors and blocklists plus manual inspection of newly-flagged APIs. Cover Your Tracks: not an evaluation at all in the scientific sense — it is a live instrument that computes entropy against its own accumulated visitor corpus and reports 'one in N browsers share your fingerprint'.
corpus_size_and_origins: FP-STALKER: 98,598 fingerprints from 1,905 distinct browser instances, collected 2015–2017 via two French extensions (AmIUnique for Firefox/Chrome) — self-selected, privacy-aware, overwhelmingly desktop, heavily French/European, and small in instance count. This is the crucial caveat: 1,905 browsers is a tiny anonymity pool, and uniqueness rises sharply as the pool shrinks. FP-Radar: top-100K websites, roughly 2010–2021, script snapshots via the Wayback Machine — a large site count but with survivorship bias (only archived scripts exist), coverage gaps for dynamically-assembled and CDN-hosted bundles, and no user population at all. Cover Your Tracks: a continuously-growing, entirely self-selected corpus of visitors who deliberately sought out an EFF privacy-test page; the population is systematically over-enriched in Tor, hardened-Firefox, extension-heavy and automation-tooling users, which biases its 'one in N' figure in both directions at once. The necessary corrective is Gomez-Boix et al., who collected 2,067,942 fingerprints on a top-15 French general-audience site and found only 33.6% of desktop and 18.5% of mobile fingerprints unique, against the >80% uniqueness reported by the self-selected studies. Any linkability figure quoted without its collection venue is unusable.
reported_precision_recall: FP-STALKER: average maximum tracking duration of >51 days for the hybrid variant, an improvement of ~36 days over the closest prior algorithm (i.e. the prior baseline linked for roughly 15 days); 26% of browser instances trackable for more than 100 days. The paper reports the hybrid variant achieving high linking precision at the cost of throughput relative to the rule-based variant [uncertain — the exact precision/recall pair and the operating threshold are not verified here]. FP-Radar: reports early detection of fingerprinting abuse in APIs not previously flagged (Gamepad, Clipboard, and the first real-world detection of Visibility API abuse for ephemeral fingerprinting), and agreement with existing detectors on known techniques; the numbers are cluster-quality and detection-lead-time rather than a clean precision/recall pair [uncertain — specific figures not verified]. Cover Your Tracks reports no precision or recall; it reports bits of identifying information per signal and an aggregate, against a denominator that is its own biased visitor corpus. Gomez-Boix: 33.6% desktop / 18.5% mobile uniqueness over 2.07M fingerprints — the only figure in this cluster measured against a general population, and the one to quote.
independent_oracle: Partially, and this is the strongest methodological feature of the cluster. FP-STALKER's linking labels come from a browser-resident extension identifier, which is genuinely independent of the fingerprint attributes being linked — the ground truth does not share assumptions with the algorithm under test. That is a real independent oracle and rare in this field. FP-Radar has no independent oracle: it validates clusters against existing fingerprinting blocklists and detectors, which encode the same prior beliefs about what constitutes fingerprinting, and against manual inspection by the authors — circular in the way most unsupervised security measurement is. Cover Your Tracks has no oracle at all; its denominator is its own traffic. Gomez-Boix is the cross-population oracle for all of them, and it contradicts the self-selected studies by a factor of roughly 2.5x on uniqueness.
evidence_independence: Mixed but better than most of this research area. FP-STALKER and Gomez-Boix come from overlapping Inria/Rennes/Lille groups — Laperdrix appears on both — so the corrective is partly self-administered, which is to its credit but not the same as adversarial replication. FP-Radar is from UC Irvine / Washington and is independent of both. Cover Your Tracks is EFF-operated and EFF-interpreted, with EFF's advocacy position on tracking; its numbers are not vendor-run in the commercial sense but are not disinterested either. Critically, the numbers that matter most commercially — how long FingerprintJS Pro, DataDome or Castle actually hold a visitor ID — are entirely vendor-asserted and unauditable; every published independent figure here is from academia, and the production systems are darker than the literature.
page_archetype_coverage: Not measured and largely not meaningful for FP-STALKER or Cover Your Tracks, which are page-agnostic — the fingerprint does not depend on whether the page is an article or a product listing. FP-Radar does have an implicit archetype dimension it never reports: fingerprinting-script prevalence is known from adjacent literature to be far higher on news, streaming, adult and e-commerce than on documentation or government sites, so FP-Radar's top-100K aggregate hides a very wide per-archetype spread in fingerprinting exposure. For this project the actionable form of that spread is: a corpus of documentation and archive pages will understate fingerprint exposure badly relative to a corpus of commercial pages, and the local measurement's 92+ distinct hosts across saved pages already hints at how commercial pages differ.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Locale is not a robustness caveat here, it is a fingerprint attribute — Accept-Language, timezone offset, and installed-font sets are among the higher-entropy fields in every study, and non-English locales are systematically MORE identifying because the anonymity pool for a given language/timezone/font combination is smaller. The self-selected corpora are French-dominated (AmIUnique, the top-15 French site), so the reported entropies are calibrated to a European population and will misstate uniqueness for CJK or RTL locales in an unknown direction. There is no script-dependence in the algorithms themselves; the bias is in the population, not the mathematics. Font-list entropy in particular is expected to behave very differently for CJK users, where a handful of large system fonts dominate [uncertain — no measurement located].
leaks_outward: Everything this cluster measures is precisely what this project's sensor discloses to every page it reads. Reading a live page in a real browser hands the page: the full HTTP header set, the full JS-visible attribute surface (canvas, WebGL, audio, fonts, screen, timezone, hardwareConcurrency, deviceMemory), and — through FP-STALKER's lens — a fingerprint that remains linkable across sessions for a median of over 50 days and, for a quarter of browsers, over 100 days. If the sensor reads a corpus repeatedly over weeks from the same profile, the pages can and will link those visits into one continuous identity. Separately, the local measurement that reading the saved corpus makes ~3,082 external requests to 92+ hosts means the disclosure is not confined to the origin under study: 92 third parties each receive a linkable fingerprint per run. That is the single largest privacy fact on this project's ledger, and it is a property of the corpus, not of the fold.
mechanism_detectability: This is the item where the project's first tension gets its evidence, and the evidence settles it against the current refusal. Nothing in FP-STALKER or FP-Radar detects automation directly, but the commercial systems built on the same attribute vectors do, and their published and reverse-engineered signal lists are specific. Marionette/WebDriver is detected in production, cheaply and universally, by: navigator.webdriver (set true by the WebDriver spec itself, one property read, no timing, no heuristic — DataDome, PerimeterX/HUMAN, Akamai Bot Manager, Cloudflare and Kasada all read it); the Marionette-specific window and document property residue; the absence of realistic pointer/keystroke entropy; and headless-mode giveaways when headless is used. navigator.webdriver is a W3C-standardised, actively-read, zero-cost boolean — it is not a theoretical channel, it is the first check in essentially every commercial anti-bot script. attachShadow patching, by contrast, is detectable only by a page that thinks to test it — via Function.prototype.toString on Element.prototype.attachShadow (a monkeypatched function does not stringify as '[native code]' unless the patch also patches toString, and a toString patch is itself detectable by the same test one level up), by comparing attachShadow.toString.name, or by timing. Function.prototype.toString-based native-code integrity checks ARE deployed in production — they appear in commercial anti-bot and anti-tamper bundles (Kasada and DataDome both ship native-function integrity checks, and the technique is standard in the obfuscated-bundle literature) — so the risk is real, not hypothetical. But it is a lower-priority, later-stage check applied to a handful of well-known targets (fetch, XMLHttpRequest, canvas getContext, toDataURL, Function.prototype.toString itself), and Element.prototype.attachShadow is not on the commonly-observed target list. Verdict on the tension: the refusal to patch attachShadow while driving Firefox through Marionette is ARBITRARY AS CURRENTLY JUSTIFIED. The detectability ordering is the reverse of the one assumed: WebDriver exposure is a standardised, universally-read boolean; attachShadow patching is a targeted integrity check that in practice is not aimed at attachShadow. If detectability were the operative reason, Marionette would have to go first. The refusal can still be defended — closed shadow roots are an author's explicit encapsulation boundary, and honouring it is a coherent ethical and stability position, and patching attachShadow is also a genuine correctness hazard because it must run before any page script and it breaks pages that themselves probe their own roots — but it must be defended on encapsulation and stability grounds, not on relative detectability.
countermeasures: Three families, all with known costs. (1) Uniformity (Tor's model): make every instance identical, which is the only approach FP-STALKER cannot defeat because there is no drift to link — but it requires accepting Tor's whole bundle including quantised viewport, which collides with this project's actuator needs. (2) Randomisation (Brave farbling): per-origin-per-session noise, which defeats naive linking but which FP-STALKER-class hybrid linkers partially recover from, since the non-farbled attributes still carry enough entropy, and which is itself a fingerprint (a browser whose canvas hash changes per session is identifiable AS a randomising browser). (3) Reduction (Firefox resistFingerprinting): freeze the high-entropy attributes to spoofed constants. For this project specifically, the highest-leverage countermeasure is not any of these but session-and-profile discipline: a fresh profile per capture run with no persistent storage caps FP-STALKER's linking at the run boundary, which converts a 51-day linkability window into a single-run one. That is cheap, costs zero fold fidelity, and is orthogonal to fingerprint hardening. Removing navigator.webdriver is available in Firefox via the marionette.enabled/dom.webdriver.enabled preferences and via profile prefs [uncertain — the exact pref names and whether they fully suppress the flag under Marionette in current Firefox are not verified].
measured_fidelity_cost: This item imposes no fidelity cost of its own; it is measurement, not hardening. What it does supply is the correct frame for the local numbers already in hand. The 0.07% null-control floor establishes that the fold's own nondeterminism is negligible, so a hardening arm's cost is genuinely attributable. The 10.49% block_trackers cost on live sites versus 0.16% on saved pages is the load-bearing result and it decomposes cleanly here: the 10.49% is not fingerprint hardening at all, it is request suppression removing content that third-party scripts would have injected, and saved pages have no such injection path, hence 0.16%. Fingerprint hardening proper (RFP, farbling) does not suppress requests and should therefore land near the 0.16% end even on live sites — which is the measurement not yet run and the one worth running: an arm that hardens fingerprint surfaces WITHOUT blocking requests, measured on live sites, to separate the two costs currently conflated under 'hardening'. The no-arm-exceeds-2.3x-floor result on saved pages is consistent with that decomposition. Profile-freshness costs nothing measurable at all and should be adopted unconditionally.
gate_state_at_capture: Not recorded by any of these, and their failure to record it is instructive. Cover Your Tracks in particular measures a browser at a single moment against a corpus with no gate-state annotation whatsoever, so its 'one in N' denominator mixes visitors who accepted consent dialogs, visitors behind VPNs, and visitors running full Tor. FP-STALKER's collection likewise carries no gate annotation. For this project the transfer is a requirement rather than a finding: given that roughly two-thirds of top sites present a consent interface, and that consent state changes which third-party scripts run and therefore which fingerprinting surfaces are touched, a capture's gate state materially changes both what content is in the fold AND what the sensor disclosed while producing it. Recording gate state is thus a privacy-ledger field, not only a fidelity field.
determinism: FP-STALKER's rule-based variant is deterministic given a fixed attribute vector and threshold set. The hybrid variant depends on a trained random forest and is deterministic only once the model is frozen; retraining on different data changes linking decisions. FP-Radar is a clustering pipeline with embedding and community-detection steps, so it is deterministic only under a fixed random seed and fixed crawl snapshot, and it is not seeded-reproducible as published [uncertain]. Cover Your Tracks is nondeterministic by construction, because its denominator corpus grows continuously: the same browser tested twice a month apart gets different 'one in N' numbers with no change to the browser.
determinism_across_versions: Poor across all three, and the drift is the subject matter rather than a defect. FP-STALKER's attribute vector is anchored to 2015-era browser surfaces (navigator.plugins, Flash-era font enumeration) that have since been removed or frozen; re-running it on 2026 browsers would use a materially different and generally lower-entropy feature set, so its 51-day figure does not transfer forward without re-measurement. FP-Radar's whole method is designed around API-surface drift and is therefore robust to it in method but tied to it in results — its clusters name the APIs of their decade. Cover Your Tracks changes its own test battery over time. The practical implication for this project's own reasoning is that all quoted entropy numbers have a shelf life of a few years, and the drift direction has been toward lower per-attribute entropy in browsers and higher reliance on behavioural and network-level signals in production anti-bot systems.
reproducibility: FP-STALKER: code released and the paper is precise about the algorithm, but the dataset is not publicly redistributable in full [uncertain], so the headline number cannot be independently re-derived — only re-measured on fresh data, which would produce a different number for legitimate reasons. FP-Radar: code public and the Wayback Machine is a stable-ish substrate, but archived snapshots do get removed and the top-100K list itself churns, so exact reproduction is not achievable; approximate reproduction is. Cover Your Tracks: not reproducible in principle, since the corpus is the live traffic. Gomez-Boix's 2.07M-fingerprint dataset is not public. Net: the field's headline figures are citable but not re-derivable, and this project should treat all of them as order-of-magnitude anchors rather than constants.
failure_modes: FP-STALKER breaks when an attribute changes discontinuously in a way its rules do not tolerate — a major browser-version jump combined with an OS upgrade, or a user switching between a hardened and an unhardened profile — producing a chain break and a spuriously 'new' browser. It also fails toward over-linking on low-entropy populations: in a fleet of identically-imaged corporate machines it will merge distinct users, and the paper's small instance count (1,905) means this regime is under-tested. FP-Radar fails on scripts the Wayback Machine did not archive, on bundles where the API keyword is constructed dynamically (obfuscated property access defeats the AST keyword extraction entirely, and fingerprinting scripts are among the most heavily obfuscated on the web), and on APIs used legitimately at the same co-occurrence signature as fingerprinting use — it cannot distinguish intent, only pattern. Cover Your Tracks fails silently whenever a user's protection makes them MORE distinctive rather than less, which the tool's own scoring only partially surfaces.
failure_visibility: Silent throughout, in the specific way that matters. FP-STALKER's chain break is invisible to the tracked user and merely costs the tracker a re-identification; the failure is loud to nobody. FP-Radar's obfuscation blindness is the worst case — the pipeline reports clean clusters over the scripts it could parse and never reports the fraction it could not, so a reader sees confident detections over an unstated denominator. Cover Your Tracks is the only one that fails semi-visibly, and only because its output is a single number a user can compare against expectation. For this project's own posture, the lesson to import is the one it already holds elsewhere: an unstated denominator is a silent failure, and any fingerprint-exposure claim the project makes about itself must state how many of the corpus's 92+ hosts were actually reachable and parsed, not just how many were seen.
scale_limits: FP-STALKER's rule-based variant is near-linear in the number of known browser instances per lookup and was explicitly designed for throughput; the hybrid variant requires a forest evaluation against candidate instances and the paper reports it as materially slower, which is why both variants exist — the accuracy/throughput tradeoff is the paper's engineering contribution. Practical trackers shard by coarse attribute buckets to keep the candidate set small, so real-world scaling is sub-linear in practice. FP-Radar's cost is dominated by crawling and AST parsing across 100K sites x a decade of snapshots, which is an offline batch cost measured in machine-weeks, and its graph clustering is superlinear in the API vocabulary, which is small. Cover Your Tracks scales with visitors and stores an ever-growing corpus.
delta_cost_model: There is a genuine and directly transferable idea here, and it is FP-Radar's. FP-Radar models a co-occurrence graph over time slices and asks what CHANGED between slices — new API keywords entering a cluster, clusters splitting or merging — which is a delta model over a symbol graph rather than a recompute. That is structurally the same shape as this project's O(delta) requirement, applied to a different alphabet. What falls outside FP-Radar's delta model is exactly what falls outside most such models: a change in the parsing layer (a new obfuscation technique) invalidates every prior slice at once, and there is no incremental repair path. FP-STALKER has no delta model; each new fingerprint is a fresh linking query against the whole candidate set. Cover Your Tracks has none. For this project the falsifiability requirement stands unmet by all three: none states what change class forces a full recompute, and FP-Radar's obfuscation-shift case is precisely the kind of out-of-model change this project must enumerate for shadow mutations, CSS-driven change, canvas, and declarative shadow DOM in the initial parse.
reanchoring_stability: This is the deepest structural analogy in the item and it is worth taking seriously. FP-STALKER is a re-anchoring problem in a different domain: an entity's identifying vector drifts continuously, and the question is whether a later observation can be bound to the same entity. Its answer — a rule set over which attributes may change, by how much, and in which combinations, backed by a learned model for the ambiguous cases — is exactly the shape of a DOM node re-anchoring policy. The measured re-anchor horizon (51 days average, >100 days for 26%) is the domain's equivalent of a measured re-anchor rate, and it is the only number in this cluster with a clean operational reading. The transfer to a trie keyed on url:xpath:markdown:content is direct: raw xpath is the fragile high-entropy attribute (it changes on any sibling insertion, like a browser-version bump), content hash is the stable low-entropy attribute (it survives structural moves but collides across duplicated content), and a FP-STALKER-shaped rule set — 'accept an anchor if xpath changed but content hash and parent tag path are stable; accept if content hash changed but xpath and preceding-sibling signature are stable; reject if both changed' — is a defensible re-anchoring policy with an explicit, measurable break rate. This is the single most adoptable thing in the item.
adversarial_exposure: This cluster preserves no page content, so it carries no invisible-content exposure of its own. Its bearing on the project's second tension is indirect but real: it establishes that a page can identify the reading agent across sessions, which means an adversarial page can serve DIFFERENT content to a known-returning agent than to a first-time visitor. That is a concealment channel that is invisible to the fold by construction, because the fold sees only what it was served, and no amount of Unicode-level or DOM-level filtering detects content that was targeted at you. The defence is not a filter but a protocol: capture from at least two independent identities (different profile, different network path) and diff the folds. A divergence between two identities on the same URL is a strong, layout-free, structure-agnostic signal of targeted serving — and it is exactly the kind of check a trie keyed on url:xpath:markdown:content can perform cheaply, since the diff is a trie-vs-trie comparison the project already has machinery for.
provenance_carrying: None of the three carries per-token provenance because none has tokens. FP-Radar carries per-API-keyword provenance to (script URL, snapshot date), which is a two-field origin tuple and is the closest analogue — and it is notably thinner than the project's own key. FP-STALKER carries per-attribute provenance to (browser instance, timestamp). The observation worth extracting is that this project's trie key (url : xpath : markdown : content) already carries strictly more provenance than any artifact in the fingerprinting literature, and that adding capture time, shadow depth and gate state to the key would make it richer than what current injection-defence proposals require. The provenance argument therefore favours the project's existing design rather than asking anything of it.
roundtrip_safety: Not applicable — no serialisation format is defined by any of these, and there is no parse-serialise cycle to be a fixed point. The nearest concept is FP-STALKER's attribute-vector canonicalisation (normalising user-agent strings and font lists before comparison), which is a one-way normalisation and explicitly lossy: two distinct raw vectors can canonicalise to the same normal form, and that collapse is the algorithm's tolerance for drift rather than a defect. That is a useful cautionary note for any content-hash normalisation this project performs — whitespace normalisation before hashing buys drift tolerance at the price of collisions, and the tradeoff must be chosen deliberately and measured, not inherited from a library default.
token_budget_and_ordering: Not applicable. These pipelines emit identifiers, scores and cluster labels, not context for a model. The only ordering concern that transfers is a governance one: if the project records fingerprint-exposure metadata alongside each capture, that metadata must live outside the SLM context window entirely — it is auditing state, not content, and it competes for the same scarce budget the fold needs. It belongs in the peripheral store keyed by address, on exactly the same footing as geometry.
representation_cost: Effectively zero for the artifacts themselves — a fingerprint vector is a few hundred bytes, a linking decision is a boolean, a Cover Your Tracks report is a page. The cost this item identifies is not in tokens but in requests and in linkability: 3,082 external requests per corpus run, each carrying a fingerprint to one of 92+ distinct hosts. If a fingerprint-exposure annotation were added per capture — say, the attribute vector actually emitted plus the third-party host list — the storage cost would be small and the audit value high, but it must not enter the fold.
what_could_be_adopted: Three specific mechanisms, in descending order of value. (1) FP-STALKER's rule-set-plus-learned-fallback architecture as the template for xpath re-anchoring policy, with its measured-break-horizon metric as the evaluation shape: state which key components may change, in which combinations, and report a measured re-anchor rate with a horizon, exactly as FP-STALKER reports tracking duration in days. (2) FP-Radar's temporal co-occurrence delta model as a template for making the O(delta) claim falsifiable — specifically its discipline of defining what a time slice is and what a between-slice change is, which forces the out-of-model change classes into the open. (3) Gomez-Boix's methodological correction as a standing rule for this project's own numbers: a measurement on a self-selected or convenience corpus overstates by ~2.5x in the fingerprinting case, and this project's saved-page corpus is a convenience corpus, so its 0.16% block_trackers cost should be presumed an understatement of the live figure — as indeed the 10.49% live number confirms. Additionally and cheaply: adopt fresh-profile-per-run as unconditional policy, since it caps cross-session linkability at the run boundary at zero fidelity cost.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: ADOPTABLE AS-IS — nothing here classifies page regions or reads page structure; FP-Radar classifies APIs, not DOM. No violation. no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE AS-IS for the fold, with an actuator-layer note — screen and viewport dimensions are fingerprint attributes that the actuator necessarily exposes, so the actuator must own a deliberate viewport choice, but nothing here asks the fold to read geometry. o_delta: ADOPTABLE AS-IS and actively useful — FP-Radar's slice-delta model is a positive template; FP-STALKER's per-query linking is not incremental and should not be copied wholesale. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS, and this item strengthens the constraint's cost — real browser plus real page means real fingerprint emission, which is a price the no-mocks stance pays and should acknowledge explicitly rather than discover later. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY, and it is the item's sharpest finding — the evidence here shows the refusal's stated justification is inverted, since navigator.webdriver is a standardised boolean read first by every production anti-bot system while attachShadow-targeted integrity checks are not in the commonly-deployed target set. The constraint should be RE-JUSTIFIED on encapsulation-honouring and page-stability grounds, which are sound, and the detectability argument should be retired or applied consistently — which would require addressing Marionette exposure first. Overall verdict: adoptable as-is as an evidentiary source and a design template; nothing here is code to import.
governance_signal_handling: None of the three reads or respects robots.txt, Content Signals, ai.txt, AIPREF, Web Bot Auth or HTTP 402. FP-Radar crawls the Wayback Machine, which raises its own layered-permission question — the Archive's robots handling is not the origin's, and consuming archived copies of scripts sidesteps the origin's current signals entirely. FP-STALKER collected via an installed extension with user consent, which is the cleanest posture in the cluster. The forward-looking relevance is inverted and important: Web Bot Auth proposes that automated agents identify themselves cryptographically, which is the deliberate opposite of fingerprint evasion, and a project that both signs its requests as a bot AND hardens its fingerprint is sending contradictory signals. That contradiction has to be resolved as policy — either identify honestly and accept differentiated service, or blend in and accept that governance signals are being read but not honoured in the identity dimension. The honest-identification path is the one consistent with this project's other commitments.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: Fingerprint attributes are personal data under GDPR — this is settled, and Article 29 Working Party Opinion 9/2014 plus the ePrivacy Directive's Article 5(3) treat device fingerprinting as requiring consent on the same footing as cookies, independently of whether an identifier is stored. The posture question for this project is not about the data it collects but about the data it EMITS: running a sensor that discloses a linkable fingerprint to 92+ third-party hosts per corpus run is the project acting as a data subject rather than a controller, so it creates no controller obligation, but it does create a real exposure for whoever operates the sensor. Where the project does become a controller is in the stored artifacts: under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026 the persistent storage of scraped page content is the regulated act, and any personal data incidentally folded from a page (author names, comment text, profile fragments) needs a lawful basis and a retention position. This item contributes one concrete requirement to that posture: if fingerprint-exposure metadata is retained per capture, it is itself a record about the operator's device and should be scoped and retained accordingly rather than accumulated indefinitely.
